about: Special relativity for TU Wien's Relativitätstheorie course of summer 2017, which left no script and no exercises: the labs follow Einstein (1905), Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper, by section and printed page, checked against the scanned original on 1 Nov 2026. The low-speed field transformation is cross-checked with Prechtl (2010), Vorlesungen über Elektrodynamik, eq. (2.43); Coulomb's field with its eq. (3.13). Maxwell's equations themselves are in the Electrodynamics Lab. Practice answers are worked by hand; tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core and fails if they disagree.

lectures.title: Kinematic part: two frames, moving clocks and rods, adding velocities
Electrodynamic part: the Maxwell–Hertz equations in a moving frame

labs.title: Minkowski diagram
labs.idea: Each frame has its own now. A moving frame's time and space axes tilt towards the light cone, and the two frames disagree on which events are simultaneous, yet agree on the interval.
labs.law: τ = γ (t − v x/c²)    ξ = γ (x − v t)    γ = 1/√(1 − (v/c)²)

equations.eq: τ = γ (t − v x/V²),  ξ = γ (x − v t),  η = y,  ζ = z
equations.note: the Lorentz transformation from K to k moving at v along x
Einstein's β, V the speed of light

equations.eq: x² + y² + z² = V² t²  ⇒  ξ² + η² + ζ² = V² τ²
equations.note: a light sphere stays a light sphere

practice.question: A frame moves at 0.6 c0. What is its Lorentz factor γ?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 902; the course left no exercise collection

labs.title: Moving clocks and rods
labs.idea: A clock moving past you runs slow and a rod moving along its length is short, both by the same factor √(1 − (v/c)²).

equations.note: axes of a moving sphere of radius R, seen from K
reading of a clock resting in k, at x = v t
the moving clock's lag, to second order

practice.question: A clock moves at 0.8 c0. How much time does it show while 10 s pass in the resting frame?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 904; the course left no exercise collection

practice.question: A 1 m rod moves along its length at 0.6 c0. How long is it, measured in the resting frame?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 903; the course left no exercise collection

labs.title: Adding velocities
labs.idea: Speeds do not simply add: two speeds below c always give one below c, and light keeps c in every frame.

equations.eq: x = (w_ξ + v) t/(1 + v w_ξ/V²),  y = √(1 − (v/V)²) w_η t/(1 + v w_ξ/V²)
equations.note: motion of a point moving at (w_ξ, w_η) in k, seen from K

equations.eq: U = √((v² + w² + 2 v w cos α) − (v w sin α/V)²)/(1 + v w cos α/V²)
equations.note: resulting speed, α the angle between v and w
light composed with any slower speed

practice.question: A ship flies at 0.5 c0 and fires a probe forward at 0.5 c0 relative to itself. How fast is the probe in the resting frame?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 906; the course left no exercise collection

labs.title: Fields of a moving charge
labs.idea: Electric and magnetic fields are one field seen from different frames: a charge at rest has only E, the same charge moving has a flattened E and a B.
labs.law: E'_y = γ (E_y − v B_z)    E'_z = γ (E_z + v B_y)    B'_y = γ (B_y + v E_z/c²)    B'_z = γ (B_z − v E_y/c²)

equations.eq: X' = X,  Y' = γ (Y − (v/V) N),  Z' = γ (Z + (v/V) M)
equations.note: electric force in k, Gaussian units

equations.eq: L' = L,  M' = γ (M + (v/V) Z),  N' = γ (N − (v/V) Y)
equations.note: magnetic force in k, Gaussian units

equations.eq: E'_x = E_x,  E'_y = γ (E_y − v B_z),  E'_z = γ (E_z + v B_y)
equations.note: the same in SI, with B = N/c

equations.eq: B'_x = B_x,  B'_y = γ (B_y + v E_z/c²),  B'_z = γ (B_z − v E_y/c²)
E' = E + v × B,  B' = B
equations.note: the low-speed form, |v| ≪ c0, in Prechtl (2010)

equations.eq: E = Q γ r/(4πε0 (γ² x² + y² + z²)^{3/2}),  B = v × E/c²
equations.note: a charge passing the origin at v, at that moment

practice.question: A frame moves at 10⁶ m/s across a pure magnetic field of 1 T. What electric field strength does it see?
practice.solution: E'_y = γ (0 − v B_z) with γ = 1.0000056, so |E'| = 1.000 × 10⁶ V/m; Prechtl's v × B gives the same to 6 digits.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 909; the course left no exercise collection
